prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level and opened new tests of gravity and fundamental constants.
For the discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductors, which established a second family of such materials.

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration, B040 for Katori and Ye and B028 for Hosono, three names in total. B040 is the one result every member ranked, and the chair's summary shows no one disputing that the physics works. My one-sentence answer to the chair's first question is this: the lattice clock is not a better comb or a better ion clock; it is the demonstration that a trapped ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in a state where the trap itself leaves the clock transition unperturbed, which is what allows the 10^-18 level, millimetre-scale redshift tests and constraints on varying constants and dark matter. That is a new regime of control over a many-body quantum system, and it has been independently reproduced and compared in several national laboratories, which is the kind of evidence from nature and not from argument that I look for. B028 is the other kind of achievement: an unexpected observation in a compound nobody expected to superconduct at 26 K, confirmed within weeks and standing for eighteen years, credited cleanly to one person who first reported it. I do not claim that the two parts share a theme; they do not. The common ground is only that each is mature, experimentally secure and cleanly attributed, and I think a prize that rests on that is better than a theme that rests on a compromise over credit.
statement.case_against: The weakest point of my own configuration is the pairing. A purist can fairly say that an atomic-physics instrument and a materials discovery are not two halves of one idea, and that I am adding B028 mainly to give condensed matter a seat. If the committee prefers a single, sharply argued part, B040 on its own is entirely defensible and I would not walk away from it. On B040 itself, the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is a real objection that the committee should answer in the citation and not wave away, and the redefinition of the second is still pending. On B028, the pairing mechanism remains unexplained, other groups quickly raised Tc, and the single-name credit leaves out Kamihara and the first Chinese extensions, so the citation must say discovery of a family and not a Tc record.

responses.point: Kroll holds that B040 is distinct from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion-control prizes because the lattice interrogates many atoms at once, that the ion clocks were beaten in stability by a wide margin, and that the pending redefinition of the second is a matter of procedure and not of whether the physics works.
responses.response: This answers my round-1 worry well. The stability argument is a statement about what the physics permits, not about an incremental gain in accuracy, and it is the reason I regard the clock as an invention in its own right and not as a third helping of metrology. I accept his point about the redefinition, and I would not treat it as a reason to wait. What I still cannot judge from my own field is early Tokyo versus JILA priority, so for my final ballot I rely on the committee's external reports for the two-name split; I am not aware of any argument in round 1 that places a third name ahead of Katori or Ye. I do ask him to say whether he would object to a citation that names the magic-wavelength scheme explicitly, since that is what separates Katori's contribution from the 2005 and 2012 work.

responses.point: Olsson joins me in pairing B040 with B028, and in her own case_against concedes that Tc was raised by other groups and that the pairing mechanism is still unexplained, so some colleagues will call the discovery clean but the physics unfinished.
responses.response: I agree with the structure she describes, and I also agree that we should not hide the unfinished physics. My reading, though, is that this does not weigh against the prize. The iron pnictides were found by experiment, their family has been studied for eighteen years and the Nobel tradition rewards the discovery of a phenomenon, as with the cuprates and the quantum Hall effect, before it is explained. I would resist her phrase only in one respect: the case for B028 should be stated as the opening of a new family of high-Tc materials and not as the record, so the citation must avoid any implication that Hosono achieved the highest Tc. If the two of us cannot persuade others that a two-part prize with no thread is acceptable, I would rather drop B028 than leave a weakly supported second part.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B061, argues that the Kane-Mele Z2 class and Molenkamp's HgTe observation are not covered by the 2016 prize, and holds that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit gap can be handled by citation wording that rests on the prediction and the observation.
responses.response: I take seriously his reasoning that the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class is distinct from the Chern and phase-transition topology honoured in 2016; that moves me away from regarding B061 as duplication, and I no longer put it down as overlap. My remaining difficulty is credit, not science. The HgTe experiment was designed around the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and a citation that says 'prediction and first observation' still invites the question of who made the prediction that was actually tested. With a three-name cap I cannot see how to repair this honestly, and that is why B061 is my first alternative and not my preferred part. If he can show a wording that does not read as a quiet omission of BHZ, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Mehlig regards B061 as arguably overdue, but states that if the committee judges that the credit cannot be drawn cleanly with three names, B040 is the better-attributed fallback.
responses.response: I value his candour, and it clarifies where the real divide lies. We agree that B061 is good physics and that its weakness is attribution; we differ only in how heavily that weighs. Since he already treats B040 as a legitimate fallback, and six members place it in their preferred configuration, I read the committee as having a shared core that B040 can provide. I would also say to him that his wish for a condensed-matter component is partly met by B028, which is a discovery that Eriksson, who ranks B061 first, lists as his second alternative alongside B040.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B040 first for its originality, reproducibility and stable two-person attribution, but is a theorist in the same AMO community and has asked for a colleague from outside AMO to test whether it reads as a fundamental result or as an instrument.
responses.response: I am happy to be that outside colleague, as a string theorist who cares most about clues from nature. My answer: a result that lets us test the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, bound the drift of constants and search for ultralight dark matter is a result about nature and not only about a machine. That is how I read it, and I am satisfied that it is physics. I would still like her draft citation wording to say what was invented, namely the magic-wavelength lattice, so that the prize names the idea and not merely 'precision'. I note her conflict disclosure and consider it handled by the fact that Kroll, Johansson and I are not close to the field.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to B040 and notes that Eriksson ranks it eighth and Johansson and I sixth, so support is broad but shallow among the condensed-matter and quantum-circuit members.
responses.response: That is a fair description of my own opening position and I should explain why it has changed. I ranked B040 sixth because of distance from the field and because of the 2005 and 2012 precedents, not because I found a scientific flaw. Having read the others, particularly the many-body and redshift arguments, I no longer hold that. I would add that the shallowness he mentions should not be read as opposition: I now regard it as one of the two parts I would defend in the final ballot, and I would encourage Eriksson to say whether his rank of eight reflects a scientific objection or only distance from the field, as the chair's own question asks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a two-part prize with no common thread, or insist on B040 as a stand-alone prize; I would accept either, but I am less sure of the second part than of the first.
Early Tokyo versus JILA priority and the claims of Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto: my recollection is unverified and I rely on the external expert reports.
Whether the citation for B028 can credit the family of materials to Hosono alone without implying a Tc record and without slighting Kamihara and the early Chinese extensions.
Whether a bounded citation for B061 can repair the BHZ and 3D-pioneer credit gap; I am currently not persuaded, but could be.
Whether proximity to the 2005 and 2012 prizes will be read by outside observers as overlap, irrespective of the scientific distinction I draw.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. My field, string theory and cosmology, is closest to B023, which I keep only as a lower alternative, and I weigh that ranking lightly. I have no tie to Katori, Ye, Hosono, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. My supervisor David Gross and my co-author Thomas Van Riet have no connection to any shortlisted candidate. As in round 1, my recollection of individual roles has not been checked against the external reports.
